theme: The city’s degradation; the final plea, restore us
readingInstruction: Read Lamentations 4:1-5:22. The last two poems describe the siege in horrifying detail and end with a communal prayer. Read the last chapter as a prayer for the people to say together, and notice the unsettled final verses.
settingTheScene: Chapter 4 is a fourth acrostic and a description of the city’s degradation: children starving, nobles in rags, prophets and priests defiled. Chapter 5 is not an acrostic, though it has 22 verses. It is a prayer for the whole community, a plea to remember what has happened and restore them. It ends without resolution, with a question. The book of Lamentations is meant to be read in its brokenness.
observation: “How the gold has grown dim, how the pure gold is changed!” (4:1).
“The tongue of the nursing infant sticks to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children beg for food, but no one gives to them” (4:4).
“The punishment of the daughter of my people has been greater than the punishment of Sodom” (4:6).
“This was for the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests” (4:13).
“Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace!” (5:1).
“Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities” (5:7).
“The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning” (5:15).
“Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old” (5:21).
interpretation:
Chapter 4 begins with a symbol of dimmed gold, used for the precious stones of the temple, now scattered at the head of every street. The precious sons of Zion, “worth their weight in fine gold,” are regarded as clay pots. Even jackals nurse their young, but the daughters of Jerusalem are cruel like ostriches in the wilderness. The poet describes starvation, even to the point of cannibalism, which Deuteronomy 28 had warned of. Nothing is spared.

The cause is again the sin of the leaders: “the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in the midst of her the blood of the righteous.” The people who should have led them to God led them astray.

The last chapter turns from description to prayer. “Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us.” The community pleads. They list their losses: inheritance turned over to strangers, orphans without fathers, water bought for money, wood sold at a price, slaves ruling over them. They acknowledge, “Woe to us, for we have sinned!” But they also affirm God’s rule: “But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.” Even in disaster, the throne of God is secure. This is the anchor of the book.

The prayer ends with a petition: “Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored!” The initiative is God’s. They cannot return by themselves. Repentance itself is a gift. And then the book ends with a question that remains open: “Or have you utterly rejected us? Are you exceedingly angry with us?” Jewish tradition repeats verse 21 after the last verse, so as not to end on a note of despair. The unsettled ending is honest. It leaves the reader waiting for the answer, which the prophets Ezekiel and Daniel, and eventually Christ, will give.
connection: Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him. Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear. Acts 3:19-20 says, “Repent, therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 7:10 says godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation. Romans 8:35-39 assures us that nothing can separate us from God’s love.
application:
Pray for a place where there is famine or war, and give practically if you can.

Use the prayer of 5:21: “Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored.” Pray it for yourself and for your church.

Rest in the truth that God’s throne endures even when ours do not.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to remember his people and restore them.
Ask him to turn you back to him.
